title: Body water and the 2% question
goal: Explain where body water sits, how to measure a water deficit, and why the 2% body mass line is both widely used and disputed.

steps.title: Where body water lives
steps.text:
About 60% of an adult's body mass is water: [total body water](g:total-body-water). It sits in three places [[c:hb-split]]:

| where | share of body mass |
|---|---|
| inside cells ([intracellular fluid](g:intracellular-fluid)) | about 40% |
| between cells ([extracellular fluid](g:extracellular-fluid)) | about 15% |
| blood [plasma](g:plasma), also extracellular | about 5% |

So a 70 kg rider holds about 42 L of water, and only about 3.5 L of it is plasma.

Sweat is less salty than body fluids (the *Sweat* lesson shows why). Losing it makes the fluid outside cells more concentrated, so water moves out of cells to even it up [[c:hb-shift]]. The loss is shared, but the plasma slice is the one the heart feels.

claims.text: At rest about 40% of body mass is intracellular fluid, 15% interstitial fluid and 5% plasma.

evidence.quote: At rest, approximately 40% of the total body mass is intracellular fluid, 15% is interstitial fluid, and 5% is intravascular fluid.

claims.text: Sweat is hypotonic, so sweating concentrates the extracellular fluid and water moves out of cells into it.

evidence.quote: Sweat is hypotonic relative to body water, so elevated extracellular tonicity results in water movement from the intracellular to extracellular (interstitial and intravascular) spaces.

steps.title: Three ways to measure hydration
steps.text:
Each tool answers a different question [[c:hb-markers]]:

- **Body mass change.** 1 kg lost in a session is about 1 L of water [[c:hb-kg-litre]]. Best for "how much did I lose today?" Weigh nude and dry, bladder emptied, before and after.
- **Urine.** [Urine specific gravity](g:urine-specific-gravity) or a colour chart, on the first urine of the morning. Cheap; colour is close enough for the field but not for the lab [[c:hb-urine-colour]].
- **Plasma [osmolality](g:osmolality).** The only marker that works well from a single sample, with no earlier value to compare with, but it needs a blood draw.

For daily checks, one position statement suggests combining three: first-morning urine, thirst and body mass. The result is your [hypohydration](g:hypohydration), or how far you are from [euhydration](g:euhydration).

claims.text: Plasma osmolality is the only good one-off marker of hydration; plasma osmolality, urine specific gravity and body mass track changes over time; first-morning urine, thirst and body mass together give the best everyday estimate.

evidence.quote: P(osm) is the only useful marker for static dehydration assessment. P(osm), U(sg), and B(m) are valid markers in the setting of dynamic dehydration assessment.
For the best estimate of hydration status in an athlete, 3 simultaneous measures are recommended: first morning urine color (or USG), thirst sensation, and body mass.

claims.text: A change in body mass during exercise is taken as a change in body water, 1 kg = 1 L, and expressed as a percentage of starting mass.

evidence.quote: A change in total body water is equated with a change in body mass (1 L = 1 kg), whereby dehydration is then expressed as a percentage of body mass in accordance with: (Δ body mass/initial body mass) × 100

claims.text: Urine colour is good enough for field use but not for laboratory precision.

evidence.quote: Ucol may be used in athletic/industrial settings or field studies, where close estimates of Usg or Uosm are acceptable, but should not be utilized in laboratories where greater precision and accuracy are required

steps.title: How big is the deficit?
steps.problem: A runner weighs 72.0 kg before a 2 h long run in the heat and 70.4 kg after (nude, dry, bladder emptied). She drank nothing. How large is her hypohydration?
steps: Mass lost = 72.0 − 70.4 = 1.6 kg, which is about 1.6 L of water (1 kg ≈ 1 L).
As a share of body mass: 1.6 ÷ 72.0 × 100 = 2.2%.
Divide by the starting mass. If she had drunk during the run, the deficit would still be the mass change alone: what she drank is already inside the 'after' weight.

steps.title: The 2% line
steps.text:
Guidelines draw a line at **2% of body mass**. The ACSM position stand sets the goal of drinking during exercise as preventing a water deficit of more than 2% [[c:hb-2pct-goal]].

Why 2%? Around there the body starts to react. Plasma osmolality has risen enough to trigger thirst and water-saving by the kidney, and heat loss and the heart come under more strain. In warm, long or hard sessions, aerobic performance can then fall [[c:hb-2pct-strain]]. The *Heat and the heart* lesson shows why less plasma means a harder-working heart.

For a 70 kg rider, 2% is 1.4 kg: about 1.4 L.

claims.text: Position stands set preventing a body mass loss of more than 2% as the goal of drinking during exercise.

evidence.quote: The goal of drinking during exercise is to prevent excessive (>2% body weight loss from water deficit) dehydration and excessive changes in electrolyte balance to avert compromised performance.
Athletic trainers should promote euhydration in this range before exercise and a body mass loss of less than 2% at the end of exercise.

claims.text: From about 2% body mass loss, thirst and renal water-saving are triggered, thermoregulatory and cardiovascular strain rise, and in many conditions aerobic performance falls.

evidence.quote: Dehydration of ≥ 2% body mass is associated with impaired thermoregulatory function, elevated cardiovascular strain and, in many conditions (e.g., warmer, longer, more intense), impaired aerobic exercise performance.

An ~ 2% increase in Posm (~ 6 mmol/kg) is commonly referenced as an osmotic threshold for compensatory renal water conservation and water acquisition (thirst), which is approximately the equivalent of ≥ 2% loss of body mass

The discussion of physiologic responses further helps inform and explain our analysis of the literature suggesting a ≥ 2% dehydration threshold for impaired endurance exercise performance mediated by volume loss.

steps.title: Does 2% really slow you down?
steps.text:
Much of the 2% evidence comes from lab rides at a **fixed intensity** until exhaustion, often in still air, by riders who *knew* they were dry. Two meta-analyses by Goulet found that in **time trials**, losses up to about 4% did not lower power; only fixed-intensity tests showed harm from 2% [[c:hb-goulet]].

Knowing you're dry may itself slow you, so some labs hid it, giving water by vein or stomach tube [[c:hb-blinded]]:

| study | deficit | result |
|---|---|---|
| Cheung 2015: 20 km TT, 35 °C | 3% | no change |
| Wall 2013: 25 km TT, 33 °C, strong headwind fan | 3% | no change |
| James 2017: 15 min test, 34 °C | 2.4% | 8% less work |

All used 7–11 people. The question is open.

claims.text: Meta-analyses found that exercise-induced dehydration up to about 4% did not reduce time-trial performance, while it reduced performance in fixed-intensity protocols.

evidence.quote: Compared with euhydration, EID increased (0.09±2.60%, (p=0.9)) EP under time-trial exercise conditions, whereas it reduced it (1.91±1.53%, (p<0.05)) with NEV exercise protocols.
Compared with euhydration, EID (up to 4% BW loss) does not alter cycling performances during out-of-door exercise conditions

claims.text: Blinded studies disagree: two found no effect of about 3% hypohydration on time-trial performance in the heat, one found 2.4% hypohydration cut work in a 15 min test.

evidence.quote: Within the range of up to 3% body mass loss, neither the physiologic effects from lowered hydration status nor the perception of thirst, separately or combined, affected sustained submaximal exercise performance in the heat for a healthy and fit population.

When well-trained cyclists performed a 25 km cycling time trial under ecologically valid conditions and were blinded to their hydration status, performance, physiological and perceptual variables were not different between trials.
These results provide novel data demonstrating that exercise performance in the heat is impaired by hypohydration, even when subjects are blinded to the intervention.

debate.question: Does losing 2–4% of body mass slow endurance performance in real racing?

sides.position: Yes: from about 2%, heat and heart strain rise and performance falls, especially in the heat; even blinded, 2.4% hypohydration cut work by about 8%.
Not in race-like conditions: in time trials with airflow, even when blinded, losses up to 3–4% did not lower power, so drinking to thirst is enough.

points: About 60% of body mass is water: about 40% inside cells, 15% between cells and 5% in plasma.
Body mass change gives the loss in a session (1 kg ≈ 1 L, as % of starting mass); first-morning urine tracks day to day; plasma osmolality is the best one-off marker.
Guidelines aim to keep losses under 2% of body mass, the point where thirst, kidney water-saving and heat and heart strain rise.
Whether 2–4% slows real racing is disputed: time trials and two blinded studies found no effect, another blinded study found 8% less work.

variants.stem: About how much total body water does a 65 kg triathlete hold?

options.text: About 39 L
options.why: Right: about 60% of body mass, 0.60 × 65 = 39 L.

options.text: About 26 L
options.why: That is 40%: only the water inside cells. Add the 15% between cells and 5% in plasma.

options.text: About 3.3 L
options.why: That is 5%: only the plasma, a small slice of total body water.

options.text: About 10 L
options.why: That is 15%: only the fluid between cells.

variants.solution: Total body water ≈ 60% of body mass = 0.60 × 65 kg = 39 kg ≈ 39 L.

variants.stem: About how much water sits inside the cells of an 80 kg cyclist?

options.text: About 32 L
options.why: Right: intracellular fluid is about 40% of body mass, 0.40 × 80 = 32 L.

options.text: About 48 L
options.why: That is 60%: all body water, not just the part inside cells.

options.text: About 16 L
options.why: That is 20%: the water outside cells (15% between cells plus 5% plasma).

options.text: About 4 L
options.why: That is 5%: only the plasma.

variants.solution: Intracellular fluid ≈ 40% of body mass = 0.40 × 80 kg = 32 L.

variants.stem: A cyclist sweats 2 L on a hot ride and drinks nothing. Where does the lost water come from?

options.text: From fluid outside cells and, as that gets more concentrated, from inside cells too
options.why: Right: sweat is less salty than body fluids, so the fluid outside cells gets more concentrated and pulls water out of cells. The loss is shared.

options.text: Only from blood plasma, because sweat glands draw on the blood
options.why: Plasma does lose water, but it is refilled from the fluid between cells and from inside cells; the loss is spread out.

options.text: Only from inside cells, because that is where most of the water is
options.why: Sweat is made from the fluid outside cells; cells give up water only as that fluid gets more concentrated.

options.text: From the gut contents, so cells and blood stay as they were
options.why: The gut holds little spare water; a 2 L loss always comes from body fluid compartments.

variants.stem: A cyclist wants to know how much water she loses on her usual 3 h summer ride. Which measure answers that best?

options.text: Nude body mass before and after the ride
options.why: Right: within a session, 1 kg of mass lost is about 1 L of water. This is the tool for 'how much today?'

options.text: The colour of her urine after the ride
options.why: Urine colour gives a rough idea of how concentrated urine is, not how many litres were lost.

options.text: One plasma osmolality sample before the ride
options.why: That tells her starting state, not what she lost during the ride.

options.text: The number of bottles she drank
options.why: Intake is not loss; she may have drunk much less (or more) than she sweated.

variants.stem: A doctor sees a triathlete for the first time and has one blood sample, with no earlier weights or tests. Which marker best tells whether he is hypohydrated?

options.text: Plasma osmolality
options.why: Right: it is the only marker that works well from a single sample, with nothing to compare against.

options.text: Body mass
options.why: Body mass only shows a deficit when compared with an earlier, normal value.

options.text: Urine colour
options.why: Urine colour is a rough field guide and is best on first-morning urine, tracked over days.

options.text: Resting heart rate
options.why: Heart rate changes with many things (sleep, illness, stress) and isn't a hydration marker.

variants.stem: A runner weighs 60.0 kg before a 90 min run and 58.8 kg after. She drank 0.4 L during the run. What is her hypohydration, as % of body mass?

options.why: Right: (60.0 − 58.8) ÷ 60.0 × 100 = 2.0%. The drink is already inside the 'after' weight.
This adds the 0.4 L drunk: (1.2 + 0.4) ÷ 60 = 2.7%. That gives sweat lost, not the water deficit left.
1.2 is the mass lost in kg, not a percentage of body mass.
1.2 ÷ 60 = 0.02 is a fraction; multiply by 100 to get a percentage.

variants.solution: Deficit = 60.0 − 58.8 = 1.2 kg. As % of starting mass = 1.2 ÷ 60.0 × 100 = 2.0%.

variants.stem: A cyclist weighs 75.0 kg before a 3 h ride and 73.2 kg after. He drank 0.6 L. What is his hypohydration, as % of body mass?

options.why: This adds the 0.6 L drunk: (1.8 + 0.6) ÷ 75 = 3.2%. That is sweat lost, not the deficit left.
1.8 is the mass lost in kg, not a percentage.
1.8 ÷ 75 = 0.024 is a fraction; multiply by 100.

variants.solution: Deficit = 75.0 − 73.2 = 1.8 kg. As % of starting mass = 1.8 ÷ 75.0 × 100 = 2.4%.

variants.stem: A triathlete weighs 68.0 kg before a brick session and 67.0 kg after. She drank 1.0 L. What is her hypohydration, as % of body mass?

options.why: This adds the 1.0 L drunk: 2.0 ÷ 68 = 2.9%. That is sweat lost, not the deficit left.
1.0 is the mass lost in kg, not a percentage.
1.0 ÷ 68 = 0.015 is a fraction; multiply by 100.

variants.solution: Deficit = 68.0 − 67.0 = 1.0 kg. As % of starting mass = 1.0 ÷ 68.0 × 100 = 1.5%.

variants.stem: What happens in the body around a 2% body mass loss that makes guidelines use it as a line?

options.text: Thirst and kidney water-saving kick in, and heat and heart strain rise
options.why: Right: plasma osmolality has risen about 2%, enough to trigger thirst and water-saving; thermoregulatory and cardiovascular strain rise.

options.text: Blood sodium falls below the normal range
options.why: Sweat is less salty than plasma, so losing it raises blood sodium; low sodium comes from drinking too much.

options.text: Sweating stops to save the water that is left
options.why: Sweating carries on; hypohydration only delays and slightly reduces it.

options.text: Plasma is fully emptied and cells give up their water
options.why: Plasma falls by a small fraction, and cells give water from the start; nothing is emptied at 2%.

variants.stem: A runner weighs 68.0 kg before a long run. Below what post-run body mass has she lost more than 2%?

options.why: This takes 2% as 2 kg. The line is a percentage of body mass.
This uses 0.2% (0.136 kg): a decimal slip. 2% is 0.02 × 68.
This adds 2% instead of taking it away; a deficit lowers body mass.

variants.stem: A cyclist weighs 82.0 kg before a hot race. Below what post-race body mass has he lost more than 2%?

options.why: This takes 2% as 2 kg. The line is a percentage of body mass.
This uses 0.2% (0.164 kg): a decimal slip.
This adds 2% instead of taking it away.

variants.stem: Goulet's meta-analysis found harm from 2% hypohydration in fixed-intensity rides to exhaustion but not in time trials. What does that suggest about the 2% rule?

options.text: It rests mainly on test formats that are less like racing
options.why: Right: Goulet concluded the 2% rule came from fixed-intensity protocols and doesn't carry over to time-trial, out-of-doors conditions.

options.text: Time-trial riders lost less water, so they weren't really dry
options.why: Both kinds of study included losses around 2% and above; the difference was the test format.

options.text: Fixed-intensity tests are more precise, so racing must suffer too
options.why: Precision isn't the issue: a ride to exhaustion at a set power measures something different from a race.

options.text: Hypohydration clearly speeds up time trials by cutting body mass
options.why: The time-trial effect was +0.09% and not significant: no change, not a gain.

variants.stem: Why did Cheung, Wall and James give water by vein or stomach tube so riders couldn't tell their hydration state?

options.text: Knowing you're dry can change effort and pacing and bias the result
options.why: Right: blinding separates the effect of the water deficit itself from the effect of knowing about it.

options.text: Fluid by vein reaches the muscles faster than drinking
options.why: Speed of delivery wasn't the point; the aim was to hide which trial was which.

options.text: To stop riders from drinking extra during the test
options.why: Intake was controlled in all trials anyway; the tube or vein hid the amount from the rider.

options.text: To make the riders sweat less in the heat
options.why: Giving water by vein doesn't reduce sweating; it hides the hydration state.

variants.stem: Wall 2013 found 3% hypohydration didn't slow a blinded 25 km time trial in 10 well-trained cyclists. What most limits using it to plan drinking for a 6 h Ironman bike and run?

options.text: A short test in 10 trained cyclists says little about losses that build over many hours
options.why: Right: a 25 km TT lasts under an hour; small sample, one sport, one duration. Longer events can bring bigger deficits and other problems.

options.text: Blinding makes the results apply to any event length
options.why: Blinding removes one bias; it doesn't make a short test represent a long one.

options.text: A crossover design can't show cause and effect
options.why: A randomised crossover is a strong design for cause and effect; the limit is who and what was tested.

options.text: The strong fan made it less realistic than still-air lab tests
options.why: The fan mimics riding airflow: it made the test more realistic, not less.
